content: Vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (VRSA) infections are extremely rare. If you suspect you have an infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), it is essential to consult a healthcare provider promptly. Vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VISA) and VRSA are specific types of S. aureus bacteria that have developed resistance to vancomycin, an antibiotic commonly used to treat serious bacterial infections. However, resistance to vancomycin in S. aureus is exceedingly uncommon. Infections caused by VISA or VRSA may present as skin conditions such as pimples, boils, or other localized skin issues. VRSA can also lead to wound infections. Certain individuals are at higher risk of developing VRSA infections. These include people with underlying health conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease, individuals with medical devices like catheters inserted into their bodies, those with a history of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections, and individuals who have recently used vancomycin or other antibiotics. Although there has been no documented transmission of VRSA in the United States, it is theoretically possible for VRSA to spread in ways similar to MRSA. This includes close physical contact with infected individuals or exposure to contaminated materials, such as bandages. To prevent the spread of VISA/VRSA, caregivers, visitors, and anyone in close contact with infected patients should maintain proper hand hygiene by washing hands thoroughly with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand sanitizers. They should avoid contact with other people’s wounds or materials contaminated by wounds and adhere to the hospital’s recommended precautions when visiting patients. Healthcare providers must follow strict infection control practices, such as wearing gloves when handling infectious body substances and practicing proper hand hygiene, to minimize the risk of spreading these bacteria to other patients. Clinical diagnostic testing is available to confirm whether a patient has a VISA or VRSA infection. These tests also assist healthcare providers in selecting the most appropriate treatment. In the United States, all VISA and VRSA isolates identified to date have been susceptible to several FDA-approved antibiotics, which can be used for effective treatment and recovery. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is actively involved in tracking VRSA infections through programs such as the Emerging Infections Program and the National Healthcare Safety Network. Data on VRSA infections is also accessible through the Antibiotic Resistance (AR) & Patient Safety Portal. The CDC collaborates with health departments, federal agencies, healthcare providers, and patients to prevent VRSA infections and limit the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Additional resources, including laboratory tools and guidelines for investigating and controlling VRSA, are available to support healthcare professionals in managing these infections.
